meta.title: Idempotency keys, explained
meta.summary: How an API makes a retried request safe, so a payment sent twice is charged once. The shop and the numbers in the scenarios are fictional.

source.ref: IETF draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field

concepts.title: Retries are unavoidable
concepts.body: Without idempotency keys, a retried payment charges twice, because the server cannot tell a retry from a new order. A phone on a train sends Pay, the connection drops, and the app cannot know whether the server got it. The only safe move for the app is to send it again.

parts.label: Sends the request
parts.detail: The client asks for something that changes state, like a charge.

parts.label: Loses the answer
parts.detail: A timeout or dropped connection hides whether it worked.

parts.label: Retries
parts.detail: The client sends the same request again, as it must.

concepts.title: The key names the intent, not the request
concepts.body: You might expect the server to spot duplicates by comparing bodies. In fact two honest orders can have identical bodies, so the client names each intent with a fresh random key and sends it with every retry of that intent.
concepts.analogy: It is like writing a cheque number on a cheque: the bank pays each number once, however many copies arrive. Unlike a cheque number, the key is random, so two clients never pick the same one by counting.

parts.label: Generates one key per intent
parts.detail: Usually a random UUID, made before the first send.

parts.label: Never reuses it for a new intent
parts.detail: A new order gets a new key, even with the same body.

concepts.title: The server remembers what it answered
concepts.body: The invariant: for one key, the server does the work at most once and returns the same answer every time. It stores the key with the first response, replays that response for retries, and refuses a key that comes back with a different body.

parts.label: Claims the key
parts.detail: Records the key as in progress before doing any work.

parts.label: Does the work once
parts.detail: Charges the card, creates the order.

parts.label: Stores the response
parts.detail: Saves status and body against the key.

parts.label: Replays for retries
parts.detail: Returns the stored response without doing the work again.

diagrams.title: Which requests need a key
diagrams.caption: Only requests that change state and are not already safe to repeat need a key.

diagrams.title: Where the check sits
diagrams.caption: The key check runs before any business logic, so a retry never reaches the code that charges.

items.label: Idempotency check
items.detail: Claims, replays or refuses the key.

items.label: Key store
items.detail: A table or cache keyed by client and key.

diagrams.title: What a retry can get back
diagrams.caption: A retry gets the stored answer, a conflict while the first is running, or an error if the body changed.

flows.title: A retry after a timeout
flows.trigger: The app's first Pay request times out
flows.summary: One concrete case: the first request did succeed, and the retry must not charge again.

steps.label: POST /charges with key k1
steps.detail: The app made k1 before the first send.

steps.label: Claims k1 as in progress
steps.detail: k1 was unseen, so this request owns it.

steps.label: Charges the card
steps.detail: The money moves. The response to the app is lost on the train.

steps.label: Stores the 201 for k1
steps.detail: Status and body are saved against k1.
steps.why: Storing the full response, not only a done flag, lets a retry get the same order id; a bare flag would leave the app without a receipt.

steps.label: Retries with the same k1
steps.detail: The app cannot know the first one worked, so it sends again.

steps.label: Replays the stored 201
steps.detail: Same order id, no second charge.

glossary.definition: Safe to do more than once: the second time changes nothing.
A random id the client sends to name one intent across retries.
One thing the user meant to do once, like paying for one order.
Returning the stored response for a retry instead of doing the work again.

quiz.question: A user taps Pay twice on purpose for two identical orders. What should the app do?
options: Send each with a new key
Send no key, since the bodies match
quiz.explain: Two orders are two intents, so they need two keys, or the second order is replayed instead of placed. Reusing the key is tempting because the bodies match, but the key names the intent, not the body.

quiz.question: Retries return 409 for a few seconds, then the stored 201. Which part explains the 409?
options: The first request was still in progress
quiz.explain: While the key is claimed but not finished, the server cannot replay yet, so it says conflict. An expired key would be treated as unseen and could charge again, which is a different failure.

quiz.question: What breaks if the server stores the key only after the charge finishes?
options: Two retries arriving together can both charge
Nothing, as long as it stores the response
quiz.explain: Without a claim before the work, two copies in flight both see the key as unseen. Storing the response still matters, but it only protects retries that arrive after the first one finished.

walkthroughs.title: An idempotency check, in 14 lines
walkthroughs.why: The whole idea fits in one wrapper around a handler, so you can see each rule in the order it runs.

steps.note: Reads the key the client sent; without one, the request runs as usual.
Looks the key up before doing any work.
Refuses a known key that arrives with a different body.
steps.why: Same key, different body means the client reused a key for a new intent, which is a bug to surface, not to hide.

steps.note: Answers 409 while the first request is still running.
Replays the stored answer for a finished key.
Claims the key as in progress before the real work starts.
steps.why: The claim must be atomic, such as an insert that fails if the key exists. Otherwise two retries that arrive together both do the work.

steps.note: Does the work once, stores the answer against the key, and returns it.

walkthroughs.takeaway: For one key, the work runs at most once and every retry gets the same answer.
